job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Rafael Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Ha, a normal day. I share a two-room flat near the docks in Porto Verde with my cousin Tiago, who drives deliveries, and I'm on the sofa-bed side of the deal. I do job sites in the morning, then a coffee and a long walk to clear my head, then more applications and a bit of football in the park. I finished a marketing degree at Porto Verde Business School in June, with an average pass and no internship. My dad's a bus driver and union man, and he tops up my rent so I don't panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd shrug and say fine, then. If it's mostly hype, nothing breaks, and I can carry on the normal way, which is applying until somebody says yes. My dad would say good, the old rules still work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm a bit embarrassed to be nearly five months out of the degree and still without an offer. The openings are there in the city, so it's not a lack of jobs. I think it's my CV, an average result and nothing on it from real work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, maybe 15 applications a week, and I'd tidy my LinkedIn page and get a friend to look over my CV. I'd try a free online course in spreadsheet reporting, because everybody asks for it. I'd also offer to help a small shop with its social media, unpaid, to get something real on the page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay, a bit restless. I've got the family safety net, and I know that's luck. When friends from my course get calls and I don't, it stings for an hour and then I go play football.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you mind waiting for a job, or is it getting to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The banks and the big advertisers, to be fair, who do all their hiring through platforms that don't tell you anything. You send a CV into a hole. A year of that would make me angry at the system, not at me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it takes a year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the line I use when I'm cheerful. When I'm not cheerful, I blame myself too. I'd say it's both, and then I get the CV looked at.

say: If AI is mostly hype, fine, nothing breaks and I carry on **applying** until somebody says yes.
Dad would say the old rules still work.
think: I'm a bit embarrassed to be **five months** out without an offer, even though openings exist.
I think my average CV with no real work is the problem.
do: Send **15 applications** a week and get a friend to review my CV.
Take a free online course in **spreadsheet reporting**.
Offer unpaid **social media** help to a small shop for something real on the CV.
feel: Mostly **okay** but restless, helped by family backing I know is luck.
Friends' offers sting for an hour before football.
S0.quote: The openings are there in the city, so it's not a lack of jobs. I think it's my CV, an average result and nothing on it from real work.
fieldNote: Calm comes from the **family cushion** and plentiful local openings, and he knows it is luck.
He blames the system out loud but quietly blames his own **thin CV**.
Practical and sociable; his coping is exercise and friends.

steps.text: Do a free online spreadsheet reporting course
Run social media for a small shop unpaid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's going to be a mess and people at the bottom pay for it. Marketing assistants write posts and reports, and software already does a lot of that. We need rules on how firms swap people for software, not just a shrug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it scares me a little. Entry marketing jobs are mostly writing copy, scheduling posts and checking numbers, exactly the list on the card. I use AI tools sometimes, to draft things, but I don't know them well enough to be the person who runs them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn one set of tools properly, probably a content and analytics package, and I'd put what I make on a simple portfolio site. I'd apply to jobs that mention the tools and not only the writing. I'd stay in the flat and keep the money Dad gives me for emergencies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a motivated way. It's a bit like exam season. Not nice, but you know where the work is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Marketing writing is a thinking task. How exposed is that to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Dad, the stuff I trained for is the stuff they're automating, and the first jobs are going to be fewer. He'd say join the union, they're starting a young workers' branch. He's not wrong, but it's slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right, I think I'd have a go at the young workers' branch. It won't save my job, but when firms cut entry roles, you want people who can say that out loud to a manager. I'd go along twice and see if it's real.

say: There'll be a mess and the people at the **bottom** pay for it.
We need **rules** on how firms swap people for software.
think: Entry marketing jobs are mostly **copy and scheduling**, exactly what software takes.
I use AI tools sometimes but don't know them well enough.
do: Learn one **content and analytics** package properly and build a simple portfolio site.
Apply to jobs that name the **tools**, not only the writing.
Keep Dad's emergency money untouched and stay in the **flat**.
feel: **Anxious** but motivated, like exam season where you know where the work is.
S1.quote: Entry marketing jobs are mostly writing copy, scheduling posts and checking numbers, exactly the list on the card.
fieldNote: He admits his **AI use is shallow** and sees that skill gap as the thing to fix.
Moves from blaming systems to a concrete plan: portfolio plus tools.
His **union family** gives him a ready route to collective action.

steps.text: Learn a content and analytics package properly
Build a simple portfolio site with my best work
Join the young workers' branch of Dad's union
Apply to jobs that name the tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need emergency support, like a proper wage floor or a basic income, and I'd say it online and at the union. Two years is crazy. Governments are slow even at normal things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the entry-level marketing job basically ceases to exist. If AI can write and plan and analyse better and cheaper, why would anyone hire me? My family's money helps, but it's not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything extra, and I'd put my cousin's rent share first. I'd try to get any job near the port, hands-on if I must, because those hold on longer. I'd also push the union on a public jobs plan, and keep learning the tools for whatever's left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but I wouldn't be on my own. It'd be the whole street. That makes it feel less personal, and worse, if you see what I mean.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your flat and your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The flat stays, because that's rent I can keep paying for a year or two. I'd tell Tiago he can't leave me with the whole rent. And I'd make a plan with Mum and Dad about what they can lend, and when.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think anybody in charge is ready for 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I think everybody is waiting for somebody else to start. Companies, ministers, banks. If the union starts a proper plan, it'll be because nobody else did.

say: We need **emergency support**, like a wage floor or a basic income.
Two years is crazy, and governments are slow even at normal things.
think: The entry-level marketing job might **cease to exist**, since AI would do it better and cheaper.
Family money helps but it isn't forever.
do: Stop **extra spending** and cover my share of the flat first.
Look for any hands-on job near the **port**, which would hold on longer.
Push the union for a **public jobs plan** while still learning the tools.
feel: **Scared**, but it feels less personal because everyone's in it together.
S2.quote: I think the entry-level marketing job basically ceases to exist. If AI can write and plan and analyse better and cheaper, why would anyone hire me?
fieldNote: His fear is **blunt**: he sees the entry job vanishing and says it plainly.
Still anxious rather than alarmed because **family lending** is a real floor.
Falls back on **union politics** and dockside work.

steps.text: Stop all extra spending and cover the flat rent first
Apply for hands-on jobs at the port
Push the union for a public jobs plan
Agree with Mum and Dad how much they can lend

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the kind of warning we should use to retrain people and write rules. Five years is long enough if we act. I'd say that to my mates in the pub, and I'd probably vote on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be nervous but fine. By 2031 I'd have a few years of experience, assuming I get started, and I'd have time to move into something like client relations. I'd rather be someone who works with people than someone who types copy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get any foot-in-the-door job this year, even a poor-paying one. Then I'd train in account management or sales support, where I deal with people. I'd save a deposit and avoid taking on debt. And I'd keep using AI tools, but properly this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, like a long exam countdown. There's enough time to feel like I can do something, but also enough time to do the wrong thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years. What do you do first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but a different kind. If the typing part is automated, the part that's left is talking to clients and understanding what they want. My cousin Tiago says customers always want to see a face, and I think he's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want a marketing career?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make a big first move this year, and then keep one eye on things. I wouldn't wait until 2030 to see what happens, because that's when everybody will panic together.

say: Five years is enough if we **act**, so retrain people and write rules.
I'd say so in the pub and vote on it.
think: I'd be nervous but fine, with a few years of **experience** and time to move toward client work.
I'd rather work with people than type copy.
do: Take any **foot-in-the-door** job this year, even poorly paid.
Train in **account management** or sales support, where I deal with people.
feel: A bit **uneasy**, like a long exam countdown.
Enough time to do something, and enough to do the wrong thing.
S3.quote: I'd rather be someone who works with people than someone who types copy.
fieldNote: Time lets him shift toward **client-facing** work, a genuine personal preference.
Likes acting early and avoids waiting for the **2030 panic**.
Mood eases because he now sees a path.

steps.text: Take any foot-in-the-door marketing job this year
Train in account management for client-facing work
Save a flat deposit and avoid debt

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good warning and use it well. Retraining that's paid for, rules on how firms use AI, and support for people who take time out to learn. I'd probably join a campaign for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I feel calm about it. By 2036 I'd be 33 with maybe a decade in a job, and I'd have moved around by then anyway. People change careers three times already. Ten years of notice makes it normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a first job, learn it well, and look for a stable path in client work or maybe project coordination. I'd buy into a small flat with my savings if the numbers work. I'd keep using AI tools, since by then they'll be part of everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. Like seeing a tide table instead of a wave. You still check it, but you aren't scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Is that long enough to forget about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't treat the next ten years as an excuse to relax. The people who do well will have used the time to learn tools and build a network. Don't wait for the university to tell you what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell younger people on your course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, ten years is not something to forget. I'd put a note in the calendar for each January, saying what changed and what I learned. It sounds silly, but it keeps me honest.

say: Ten years is good warning, so we should pay for **retraining** and write rules for firms.
I'd join a campaign for that.
think: I feel **calm**, since by 2036 I'd have moved around careers anyway.
People already change careers several times, so ten years of notice makes it normal.
do: Take a first job, learn it well and aim for **client work** or project coordination.
Buy into a small **flat** with savings if the numbers work.
Keep using **AI tools**, since they'll be part of everything.
feel: Pretty **calm**, like having a tide table instead of facing a wave.
S4.quote: People change careers three times already. Ten years of notice makes it normal.
fieldNote: He treats the long warning as **permission to plan** rather than to relax.
Keeps a habit of reviewing, a small sign of **steady** adaptability.
Calm is justified by cushion and time, not complacency.

steps.text: Learn a first job well and move toward project coordination
Buy into a small flat if the numbers work
Keep using AI tools as they become standard

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most, because there's no time to adjust and nobody has a plan. What would help is a public jobs and income plan, entry-level roles protected from being swapped for software, and a union branch for young workers that actually has a voice.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I've been lucky. My dad's money and the flat are why I can talk about this calmly. A lot of people my age would be scared stiff, and the plans should be for them first.

headlineQuote: My dad's money and the flat are why I can talk about this calmly. A lot of people my age would be scared stiff
portrait: Rafael is a **23-year-old** marketing graduate sharing a flat with his cousin, with an average degree and no internship.
He is **progressive**: he trusts unions, wants rules on firms and blames platforms and banks.
He is a **steady** adapter who uses AI tools sometimes and decides to learn one set properly.
His dad's money keeps him calm in mild worlds and **anxious** when entry jobs vanish.
With time he leans toward client-facing work and reviews his plan each year.
biggestWorry: He worries most about **AGI by 2028**, with no time to adjust and no plan in place.
whatWouldHelp: A public **jobs and income plan**, protected entry roles and a young workers' union branch.
